title: Verifier‑Grounded Generate‑Verify‑Repair for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Paired Mininet Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; 400 paired episodes) to evaluate whether a deterministic verifier‑grounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces operationally detectable policy‑violation errors when a hosted LLM produces device configuration sequences from operator intent in a Mininet emulation. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent reused by both baseline and guarded). Baseline success (no detected policy violation) = 196/200 (98%); guarded success = 200/200 (100%). Paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.02; preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory test). An exploratory paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) yields a 95% percentile CI = [0.005, 0.04]. Four verifier‑triggered repairs occurred (total hosted model calls = 204), giving mean extra model calls per intent = 0.02 and mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. All reported numeric values, provider‑call accounting, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are drawn verbatim from the archived execution and analysis bundle. We interpret the preregistered confirmatory result conservatively and discuss construct, internal, and external validity limits and operational implications.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation is a promising NetOps automation vector, but generative LLMs can produce mechanically detectable faults—syntax errors, topology/reachability violations, and ACL/policy mistakes—that may have operational consequences (availability loss, unintended access, or security exposure) [1], [4]. Closed‑loop generate–verify‑repair (GVR) pipelines pair an LLM generator with a deterministic verifier that checks mechanizable constraints and, if violations occur, requests localized repairs from the model [2], [3]. Prior prototypes demonstrate value of verifier‑grounded repair for mechanically checkable errors in code and domain‑specific program generation, yet open questions remain about scalability across heterogeneous vendor templates, concrete hosted‑LLM cost per avoided violation, and the interpretation of paired comparisons under shared_initial_candidate sampling semantics.

We preregistered study C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 to address these gaps with a confirmatory paired design executed in Mininet emulation. The study exercises heterogeneous synthetic vendor templates and topology patterns and enforces shared_initial_candidate semantics so that, for each intent, baseline and guarded outcomes begin from the same sampled candidate and any paired difference can only arise from deterministic validation and any permitted repair. Our primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) for producing zero operationally detectable policy violations, analyzed with the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test. All reported numbers and diagnostic traces are taken directly from the archived execution and analysis artifacts.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and NetOps‑specific reviews document rapid growth in applying LLMs to network automation while highlighting recurring evaluation gaps: benchmark provenance, verifier integration, and limited multi‑vendor emulation evidence [5], [6]. Prototype NetOps experiments and adjacent domain work show LLMs can draft device configurations but frequently introduce syntax, topology, or policy errors; generate–verify–repair or verifier‑grounded loops recur as mitigation patterns in code and domain program generation [2], [3]. NetConfEval and related efforts provide initial benchmarks for intent→configuration tasks but often lack provenance‑traced verifier pipelines and paired confirmatory designs that isolate verifier effects [4].

Our contribution situates an artifact‑grounded paired confirmatory evaluation in this landscape by (i) enforcing provenance tracing and preregistration, (ii) executing a paired design under shared_initial_candidate semantics across heterogeneous synthetic templates, and (iii) reporting precise provider and validator accounting so repair cost can be measured concretely in hosted‑LLM call counts. We avoid claims of production readiness and restrict inference to the emulated, template‑driven scope that the deterministic validator can express and check.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the design as C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 prior to any model calls (preregistration SHA‑256 = 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (probability an intent yields zero detected violations under guarded minus baseline) tested via exact McNemar two‑sided test at α = 0.05. Exploratory predeclared quantities included a paired bootstrap percentile CI for the risk difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) and descriptive cost metrics (mean extra hosted model calls per intent and mean extra calls per avoided violation).

Sampling, strata, and shared_initial_candidate semantics: The adapter deterministically selected N = 200 unique operator intents stratified across three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata). Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial sampled generation per intent was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded episodes. Under this semantics, the baseline outcome is the validator verdict on that shared initial candidate; the guarded outcome is the final guarded pipeline result after deterministic validation and any permitted repair. The preregistration explicitly declared that independent constrained‑prompt arms were not executed; therefore paired differences measure only validator/repair effects, not changes in initial sampling or prompt templates.

Model and budget constraints: The declared model recorded in the archived configuration is gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). The archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Planned budget parameters were initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1, and maximum_model_calls = 400; the execution adhered to these limits.

Deterministic validator and repair semantics: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed syntactic parsing of configuration lines, required‑command sequencing checks against per‑task required sequences, reachability/topology verification against the emulated Mininet state, and encoded ACL/policy checks derived from per‑task payload constraints. Validator outputs included structured diagnostics (violation codes, parsed command counts, required command counts) and a boolean valid flag under the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation. When violations were detected the guarded pipeline could issue up to one repair call: repair prompts were automatically constructed from the validator's localized diagnostics to request focused corrective modifications. The repair policy permitted at most a single verifier‑triggered repair per intent; repair application is recorded by validator_trace.repair_applied in the archived per‑episode artifacts.

Analysis, missingness, and deterministic accounting: The preregistered primary analysis was the exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary success indicators. The preregistration specified conservative handling of ambiguous validator outputs (treat as violations in the primary analysis) and deterministic duplicate detection exclusions; in execution no pairs were excluded and no episodes failed. Deterministic provider audit and reconciliation were performed post‑run: audited hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared_initial_generation events and 4 repair calls; cache_hit_count = 0 and cache_miss_count = 204. Stage accounting reported shared_initial_generation = 200 and repair stage = 4. These audited counts are used verbatim in Results.
sections.results:
Execution completeness and paired outcomes: The run completed as preregistered: planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200; failed_episode_count = 0. The paired contingency from analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv is n11 = 196, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (where n10 are pairs where guarded succeeded and baseline failed). Baseline success rate = 196/200 = 0.98; guarded success rate = 200/200 = 1.0; paired point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.02.

Confirmatory test and exploratory interval: The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test on the paired binary outcomes yields p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory result; do not reject at α = 0.05). The archived exploratory paired bootstrap (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) produced a 95% percentile CI for the paired risk difference = [0.005, 0.04]; the bootstrap seed and resampling configuration are recorded in analysis_log.jsonl. Because discordant counts are small (n10 + n01 = 4), bootstrap percentile intervals can be unstable; we therefore report the bootstrap interval as exploratory magnitude context while treating the exact McNemar test as the formal confirmatory inference.

Repair invocation and hosted‑call cost: Four verifier‑triggered repairs were invoked across the 200 intents (repair_calls = 4). Total hosted model calls recorded by provider audit = 204 (200 shared initial + 4 repairs), yielding mean hosted model calls per intent = 1.02 and mean extra calls per intent due to repairs = 0.02. Each recorded repair corresponded to a corrected baseline failure in the archived contingency table; therefore mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. These arithmetic derivations and provider counts are taken directly from the deterministic_reconciliation and execution_manifest artifacts.

Representative episodes and validator diagnostics: Representative per‑episode scoring artifacts (for example, execution/scoring/task‑000004‑*.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate content and identical shared initial response text files reused by both baseline and guarded conditions. For discordant pairs, validator_trace.validation_before contains explicit violation codes and localized diagnostics and validator_trace.validation_after records repair_applied = true and valid = true after the repair. Parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and difficulty pattern labels reported in validator traces (e.g., "very_hard" patterns such as "rolling_access_vlan_migration") are preserved verbatim from the archived per‑episode artifacts and substantiate the claimed contingency and repair accounting.

Statistical power context and observed baseline prevalence: The preregistered power plan targeted detecting an absolute 10 percentage point reduction with N ≈ 157 (McNemar approximation) and selected N = 200 to permit stratum descriptions. The observed baseline failure prevalence (2%) was lower than some sensitivity scenarios used in planning, reducing power to detect small absolute improvements; this explains the non‑significant McNemar result despite a positive point estimate and the small number of discordant pairs. We therefore interpret the point estimate and exploratory CI cautiously and emphasize the confirmatory p‑value as the preregistered statistical decision.
sections.discussion:
Inference under shared_initial_candidate semantics: Because a single sampled candidate per intent was shared across baseline and guarded episodes, paired improvement derives only from deterministic validator/repair actions and not from independent re‑sampling or different prompting. The preregistered design intentionally isolates the verifier/repair effect: independent first‑pass prompt or constrained‑prompt arms were not executed and therefore are not measured here.

Operational interpretation and bounded claims: Within the constrained Mininet emulation, synthetic vendor templates, and the validator's encoded rules, a small repair budget (four repairs) eliminated the mechanically detectable baseline violations. The low absolute baseline failure prevalence implies modest repair activity sufficed for this workload. These artifact‑grounded results indicate that when a suitable deterministic verifier can express required constraints and provide localized diagnostics, limited repair budgets can remove mechanically checkable faults in template‑driven emulated settings. We do not claim generalization to production hardware, other prompt families, different LLMs, or to semantic errors outside the validator's rule coverage.

Threats to validity: Construct validity—the deterministic validator covers syntactic parsing, required‑command sequencing, reachability/topology checks, and encoded ACL/policy checks, but cannot detect high‑level semantic misinterpretations not expressible in its rules. Internal validity—the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were executed and deterministically reconciled (provider_call_audit and reconciliation artifacts), which prevents attributing observed gains to prompt engineering or independent re‑sampling. Conclusion validity—small discordant counts limit power and resampling stability, making the exact McNemar test the appropriate confirmatory procedure under the preregistered design. External validity—single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), synthetic templates, and Mininet emulation limit claims about production readiness or multi‑model robustness.

Recommendations grounded in archived evidence: (1) Expand deterministic verifier coverage to formalize more semantic/policy ontologies and measure residual false negatives; (2) conduct paired designs that allow independent multi‑sample initial generations to separate prompt/template effects from validator effects; (3) evaluate multiple hosted models and versions to assess robustness to provider nondeterminism; (4) preserve provenance tracing for all provider calls and validator traces to enable independent audit. Each recommendation follows directly from observed artifact evidence and stated limitations.

Reproducibility and artifact‑grounded replication notes: The execution and analysis bundles archive core artifacts used in this manuscript: the preregistration record, model configuration record (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini; temperature = null/unset), the full provider call audit (hosted_model_call_event_count = 204; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 200, repair = 4), per‑episode validator traces, the deterministic_reconciliation summary, the analysis log specifying bootstrap_seed = 1729 and resamples = 10,000, and the paired contingency CSV. A full hash manifest and execution manifest are archived with the run; these artifacts are the direct provenance for every numeric claim in this paper. (Per track guidance, the immutable initial master prompt locator and preregistration SHA‑256 are reported in the Disclosure Statement below.)
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to measure whether a deterministic verifier plus bounded repair reduces mechanically detectable policy violations for intent→configuration tasks in a Mininet emulation. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). Guarded GVR invoked four repairs and corrected the four observed baseline violations at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02), yielding a paired risk difference estimate of 0.02 and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI = [0.005, 0.04] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). These artifact‑grounded results indicate that, for template‑driven emulated settings where a deterministic verifier can express relevant constraints, a small repair budget may suffice to eliminate mechanically detectable policy violations. The results do not establish production readiness, multi‑model generality, or coverage for semantic errors outside the validator; future preregistered, provenance‑traced evaluations should expand verifier coverage, evaluate multiple hosted models, and compare independent multi‑sample baselines.

limitations: Scope limited to Mininet‑style emulation with synthetic, provenance‑traced intent→configuration tasks; results do not generalize directly to production hardware or live operations.
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) evaluated; multi‑model generality is not established.

Deterministic validator coverage limited to mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings); higher‑level semantic or specification misinterpretations outside the validator may remain undetected.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics imply observed paired differences derive only from verifier‑triggered repair; this design does not measure effects of alternative prompting strategies or independent multi‑sample candidate selection.

Observed confirmatory effect (2 percentage points) did not reach statistical significance at α = 0.05 for N = 200 (exact McNemar p = 0.125); low baseline failure prevalence (2%) reduced power to detect small absolute improvements under some preregistered scenarios.
